title: Radha and Krishna
hookLine: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda sings their love as divine love

cards: Night in a forest by a river. Somewhere among the trees, someone is playing a flute.
In the villages nearby, the cowherd women hear it, and in the Bhagavata Purana's telling, they drop what they're doing and go, out into the dark, toward the sound.
The flute player is Krishna, the cowherd boy his devotees worship as God. Later poets give one of the women who love him a name and a story of her own: Radha.
A Sanskrit poet named Jayadeva sang their love in a long poem called the Gita Govinda.

teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna's flute calls the cowherd women, the gopis, from their homes at night. Devotional readers hear it as God's call to the soul: a sound that makes everything else seem less urgent.
The Gita Govinda tells a love story with a hurt in the middle. In spring, Krishna dances and plays with many gopis.
Radha sees, and she is wounded. She withdraws into a bower in the forest and grieves, while Krishna misses her and longs for her. A friend of Radha's carries messages back and forth.
At last Krishna comes to Radha, asks her pardon, and they are reunited.
The poem dwells on their longing and their meeting in lush, frank detail, among flowers, bees and moonlight. Devotional readers don't take it as only a romance.
For some Vaishnava devotees, Radha is the soul longing for God, or even the very power of God's own love.
Her hurt, her waiting and her reunion become a map of devotion: the ache of separation, and the joy when God comes looking. The poem is sung in worship, not only recited as literature.
Some traditions emphasize the longing; others the sweetness of the meeting. Both are there in the text.

how: Vaishnava Hindus worship Radha and Krishna together in temples and homes, and songs from the Gita Govinda and later devotional poets are sung in worship and danced in classical dance traditions.

o: Jayadeva's poem of Radha and Krishna's love
a hymn to the river where Krishna played

games.q: who does what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: plays the flute in the forest
leave their homes at the sound

s: the Gita Govinda is a love story with no conflict
Radha is wounded and withdraws; Krishna longs for her and comes back.
devotees read Radha as the soul longing for God
for some Vaishnava devotees she is the soul, or even the power of God's own love.
the poem is only recited as literature
it's sung in worship, as a map of devotion.

games.q: you're Radha. in spring you see Krishna dancing with many gopis. what do you do?
o: join the dance and forget it.
withdraw into a bower in the forest and grieve.
go home and never think of him again.
games.why: Radha withdraws, hurt. and then Krishna, longing for her, comes looking, the turn the poem builds toward.

practice: Put on a love song softly, any song from any time or place, or play one in your memory.

Listen as if you were one of the gopis hearing the flute through the trees, not judging the song, just noticing what in you leans toward it, the longing and the sweetness, and then sit in the quiet after.
If you pray, you can bring that longing into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Gita Govinda. Jayadeva's poem of Radha and Krishna's quarrel and reunion, read by devotees as the soul's longing for God answered. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Radha, Krishna's beloved in the Gita Govinda.
